newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Official says Tanzania to be major gold producer.
newsitem.headline: Official says Tanzania to be major gold producer.

text.p: Tanzania, one of the world's poorest countries, will become one of the world's biggest gold producers within a decade, a senior mining industry official said at the weekend.

Addressing an annual dinner of the Tanzania Chamber of Mines in Dar es Salaam on Saturday, chairman Samuel Lwakatare said annual investment in mineral exploration had leapt to $150 million from $500,000 less than 10 years ago.
"This expenditure is rising rapidly as more companies get the confidence to get into detailed exploration and mine development.
"From now on we should be seeing one or more new sizeable mines, especially for gold, being opened in the country each year.
"This should make Tanzania one of the major gold producers in Africa, if not the world, in less than a decade," Lwakatare said.

He said Williamson Diamonds, operating a mine in western Tanzania and now owned by South Africa's De Beers group, had just finished new mine development. "Diamond production after several years of decline has started to rise," he said.

Well-known mining industry names with prospects in Tanzania included South Africa's Anglo American, JCI, De Beers, Australian miner BHP, Canada's Sutton Resources Ltd and East Africa Mines and Ghana-based Ashanti.

Annual export earnings from mining should reach $400 million before the year 2000, and Tanzania was earning an international reputation as a country with a good investment environment, the Lwakatare said.

On a cautionary note, Lwakatare said some local authorities were imposing heavy levies on mineral revenue in addition to central government charges. Excessive bureaucracy in mines licensing, customs and immigration procedures were also impeding efficiency, he said.

The first gold mine scheduled for production will be a joint venture involving British-based Samax Resources and Australia's Resolute, expected to pour their first bar in 1998. Kahama Mining, a fully-owned subsidiary of Canada's Sutton Resources, is expected to go into production at Bulyankulu in 1999.
Most of Tanzania's gold prospects are located south of Lake Victoria, where commercial mines operated in the 1950s but later closed for economic reasons.
Minerals and Energy Minister Abdallah Kigoda said the country's mining sector could be likened to a "sleeping giant" now awaking.
A new draft mining policy would be presented to parliament in October, he said.

More than 700 prospecting licenses had been issued by the ministry while investment in mining had risen from $50 million in 1994 to a projected $200 million in 1997. Four medium-to-large-scale mines would become operational before the year 2000, Kigoda said.
